_meta.status: DEMO - NOT APPROVED FOR CLINICAL OR OPERATIONAL USE
_meta.compiled: 2026-11-15 by the ARES team from the public NASA sources listed under 'sources'
_meta.policy: Immediate actions are ONLY the protocol steps stored in protocols.json, shown verbatim. Long-term effects are limited to risks NASA itself lists, each labelled with its evidence level. ARES never generates treatments. A real system would replace this file with flight-surgeon-approved content.

evidence_levels.established-spaceflight: Recognised by NASA as a human-system risk of spaceflight
evidence_levels.spaceflight-research: Seen in NASA spaceflight research data (may be animal studies)
evidence_levels.theoretical: Plausible consequence reasoned by the ARES team; not established - for discussion with the medical officer

long_term.text: NASA tracks heart rhythm problems in flight as a recognised human risk of spaceflight.
Evidence for in-flight rhythm problems comes mainly from individual case reports; NASA's cardiovascular review noted no systematic study had been published.
If episodes keep returning, demanding tasks such as spacewalks may need to wait until the medical officer has reviewed them.

monitoring: Continuous ECG while the episode lasts; ARES re-checks every minute
Review every new episode against the astronaut's own rhythm record
follow_up: Repeat blood pressure and oxygen readings (protocol CARD-01)
Medical officer review of the saved ECG strips
prevention: Keep fluid intake and sleep on schedule
Report palpitations, dizziness or chest discomfort early
watch: Resting heart rate (Gradual changes from normal)

long_term.text: After long periods in weightlessness, astronauts can feel dizzy or faint when standing up in gravity (orthostatic intolerance) - a NASA-recognised risk on return to gravity.
NASA lists cardiovascular health and performance as a human-system risk area for exploration missions.
A resting heart rate that keeps rising while blood pressure falls could mean lower fitness or fluid loss, and may reduce exercise capacity on arrival at Mars.

monitoring: Daily resting heart rate and blood pressure compared with the astronaut's own baseline
ARES drift table updates every mission hour
follow_up: Medical officer review if the change lasts more than a few days
prevention: Keep the exercise programme and fluid intake on plan

respiratory.title: Low blood oxygen or fast breathing

long_term.text: NASA lists reduced crew health and performance due to low-oxygen atmospheres (hypoxia) as a human-system risk.
Repeated or prolonged low-oxygen episodes could affect concentration and work performance during the mission.

monitoring: Blood oxygen and breathing rate every minute until back in the personal band
Check cabin air readings at the same time (CO2, O2)
follow_up: Re-measure with a backup oximeter (protocol GEN-01)
Medical officer review of the episode
prevention: Keep cabin atmosphere within limits; report breathlessness early

infection.title: Fever-like change (temperature, heart and breathing up)

long_term.text: Spaceflight changes how the immune system works; NASA lists adverse health events due to altered immune response as a human-system risk.
In a small closed cabin an untreated infection could spread to other crew members.

monitoring: Temperature, heart rate and breathing every minute while raised
follow_up: Record symptoms in the clinical log

long_term.text: NASA lists kidney stone formation as a spaceflight risk; low fluid intake is a known contributor.
NASA lists dizziness on standing (orthostatic intolerance) on return to gravity as a risk; low fluid volume makes it worse.

monitoring: Heart rate and blood pressure each cuff reading
prevention: Planned fluid intake, especially around exercise

long_term.text: Astronauts commonly experience sleep deprivation and body-clock disturbance in flight; NASA lists performance decrements and health effects from sleep loss as a human-system risk.
Slower reaction times raise the chance of errors in critical tasks.

monitoring: Reaction time and alertness test (PVT-B) daily
Sleep hours from the wrist sensor every day
follow_up: Countermeasure review in protocols FAT-01 / BEH-01
Private medical-officer conversation if the watch status lasts several days

long_term.text: NASA lists adverse health outcomes from space radiation (cancer, heart and nervous-system effects) as a human-system risk.
NASA limits career radiation exposure to 600 mSv.
ARES measures dose only; it does not estimate the biological effect on any individual.

monitoring: Cumulative dose versus the career limit
follow_up: Record the event dose for each crew member
prevention: Storm shelter during solar particle events (protocol RAD-01)

long_term.text: NASA sets cabin CO2 limits (3 mmHg 1-hour average) because higher levels affect crew health and performance.
If the CO2 removal system keeps degrading, symptoms could spread across the whole crew.

monitoring: Cabin CO2 every minute; 1-hour and 7-day averages

long_term.text: Frequent false alarms can make a crew ignore real ones (alarm fatigue).

monitoring: Signal quality of every sensor, every minute
follow_up: Re-seat or replace the sensor; confirm with a backup device (protocol GEN-01)

musculoskeletal.title: Muscle and bone changes in weightlessness

long_term.text: NASA lists bone fracture due to spaceflight-induced bone changes as a human-system risk.
In NASA mouse studies, flight changed the muscle-fibre make-up of the calf (soleus) and thinned the tibia's outer bone layer.

monitoring: No onboard muscle or bone measurement in this prototype
follow_up: Bone and muscle checks on return (outside ARES)
prevention: Daily resistance and aerobic exercise programme

long_term.text: NASA lists kidney stone formation as a spaceflight risk.
A single changed lab value is not a diagnosis; repeated changes need medical-officer review.

monitoring: Repeat the lab test at the next opportunity
follow_up: Compare with the astronaut's own pre-flight values

bone_density_loss.title: Average bone-density loss in weight-bearing bones during spaceflight

not_applicable.skull: Not weight-bearing; spaceflight studies do not report this loss for the skull.
not_applicable.arm_bones: Not weight-bearing; the published average rate does not apply.
not_applicable.ribcage: Not a weight-bearing site covered by the published average.
not_applicable.shoulder_girdle: Not a weight-bearing site covered by the published average.
not_applicable.skeleton_other: No published average for this group of bones.

bone_density_loss.basis: On average, weight-bearing bones such as the spine and hips lose 1-1.5% of their density per month on 4-6-month missions (NASA). ISS measurements: about 0.9%/month at the spine and 1.4-1.5%/month at the hip (Lang 2004). It is unknown whether the rate continues on longer missions; exercise countermeasures reduce it.
bone_density_loss.caveat: Population average for crews before modern countermeasures were fully in use - NOT a measurement of this astronaut. Bone density can only be measured on the ground (DXA/QCT before and after flight).
